questions.question: Which best matches the demographic-parity definition for groups A=a and A=a'?
options: Equal true-positive and false-positive rates across groups conditioned on the true outcome -- this is the equalized-odds criterion, not demographic parity
Equal predictive value across groups, so a positive prediction means the same thing regardless of group -- this is conditional use accuracy equality
Equal Lipschitz constant across groups in the decision map's similarity metric -- this is the individual-fairness criterion, not a group criterion
Equal acceptance rates across groups regardless of the true outcome: P(Y=1 | A=a) = P(Y=1 | A=a') for every pair of groups
questions.explanation: The lesson defines demographic parity as equal acceptance rates across groups: P(Y=1 | A=a) = P(Y=1 | A=a') for all groups a, a' -- distinct from equalized odds, conditional use accuracy equality, and individual fairness's Lipschitz condition.

questions.question: What does the Chouldechova / Kleinberg-Mullainathan-Raghavan 2017 impossibility result say?
options: Group fairness is always achievable simply by re-weighting the training examples before fitting the classifier on the fully labeled dataset
Under unequal base rates, demographic parity, equalized odds, and conditional use accuracy equality cannot all hold simultaneously
Counterfactual fairness implies demographic parity for any causal graph, so satisfying one automatically satisfies the other
Individual fairness automatically implies counterfactual fairness, regardless of which similarity metric or causal DAG is chosen
questions.explanation: The lesson states the 2017 impossibility result: under unequal base rates between groups, demographic parity, equalized odds, and conditional use accuracy equality cannot all be satisfied simultaneously -- it is not fixed by re-weighting, and it says nothing about implications between the individual/counterfactual families.

questions.question: Dwork et al. 2012 define individual fairness via:
options: Demographic parity computed at the individual level instead of aggregated across demographic groups in the population
Equal predictive accuracy across protected groups, measured the same way as the conditional use accuracy equality criterion
A Lipschitz condition on the decision map relative to a task-specific similarity metric, so similar individuals get similar decisions
A causal DAG in which the decision changes whenever a sensitive attribute is counterfactually intervened upon
questions.explanation: The lesson defines individual fairness (Dwork et al. 2012) as a Lipschitz condition |f(x) - f(x')| <= L * d(x, x') on the decision map relative to a task-specific similarity metric d, meaning similar individuals must get similar decisions -- not a group-level statistic and not a causal-DAG requirement.

questions.question: Counterfactual fairness (Kusner et al. 2017) requires:
options: No causal assumptions at all, since the fairness criterion is purely statistical and defined only on observed data
Equal Lipschitz constants for all demographic groups under the individual-fairness similarity metric d
Only group-level statistics, such as acceptance rates, true-positive rates, and predictive value across groups
A causal DAG; the decision is unchanged when the individual's sensitive attribute is counterfactually altered
questions.explanation: The lesson defines counterfactual fairness (Kusner et al. 2017) as requiring a causal DAG under which a decision is unchanged when the individual's sensitive attribute is counterfactually altered -- the decision is only as justified as the DAG, unlike the purely statistical group criteria.

questions.question: Why do backtracking counterfactuals (arXiv:2401.13935) matter for legal compliance?
options: Instead of intervening on a protected attribute, they ask which combination of actual features would have produced the counterfactual outcome
They eliminate any need for a causal model whatsoever, replacing the DAG entirely with a purely statistical group-fairness test
They replace embedding-based and probability-based bias metrics entirely with a single unified generated-text benchmark
They prove that the Chouldechova / Kleinberg-Mullainathan-Raghavan impossibility theorem does not hold under unequal base rates
questions.explanation: The lesson explains that traditional counterfactuals require intervening on a legally protected attribute, which classification law treats as problematic; backtracking counterfactuals instead ask which combination of the individual's actual features would have produced the counterfactual outcome, sidestepping that objection -- they don't remove the causal model, replace bias metrics, or overturn the impossibility theorem.

questions.question: What does the ICLR Blogposts 2024 philosophical reconciliation argue?
options: The base-rate impossibility theorems are fully and permanently resolved once the training data is re-weighted by group
With an explicit causal graph, satisfying certain group-fairness measures entails counterfactual fairness too
Group fairness and counterfactual fairness are provably unrelated criteria sharing no causal structure whatsoever
Only individual fairness is philosophically justifiable, and the other two families should be abandoned entirely
questions.explanation: The lesson summarizes the ICLR Blogposts 2024 reconciliation as showing that, given an explicit causal graph, satisfying certain group-fairness measures entails counterfactual fairness -- the apparent opposition between the fairness families is partly an artifact of leaving the causal model implicit, though it does not resolve the base-rate impossibility theorems.
